message.content:
Read ONE blog post in full and extract what it constrains about building an analytical data platform.

Fetch and convert it to text with exactly these commands:

  cd /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-adss-2026-09-07/45a0041f-5559-570b-bd39-1d1517807233/scratchpad/blog && curl -sSL --max-time 60 "https://blog.daana.dev/blog/context-isnt-enough" -o "context-isnt-enough.html" && node extract.js "context-isnt-enough.html" > "context-isnt-enough.txt" && wc -c "context-isnt-enough.txt"

Then read /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-adss-2026-09-07/45a0041f-5559-570b-bd39-1d1517807233/scratchpad/blog/context-isnt-enough.txt IN FULL with the Read tool (or cat). Do not skim, do not use WebFetch, do not summarize from the title. If the .txt is under 1500 characters the extraction failed — retry by running node extract.js on the raw html without the <article> isolation, or curl the page again.

Context you are serving: someone is about to BUILD the three-layer architecture this blog describes — DAS (data according to system), DAB (data according to business), DAR (data according to requirements) — using dlt for ingestion, a tool called daana-cli for the DAB focal model, and a generated Unified Star Schema for DAR. Your extraction is the only way this post reaches them. Be concrete and faithful.

Rules:
- mandates: only what the post actually says. Do not invent, do not generalize beyond the text.
- artifacts: anything NAMED — YAML keys, CLI commands and flags, schema names, table/column naming rules, SQL constructs, directory layouts, type mappings. Copy them verbatim. This is the highest-value field; be exhaustive.
- quotes: verbatim only, no paraphrase.
- openQuestions: places where the post says "you must decide X" or clearly leaves a choice open.
- If the post is an interview or company story with little build guidance, say so honestly via relevance:'low' and keep mandates short rather than padding.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

Published onTuesday, June 23, 2026

# Context Isn't Enough: Agentic Analytics Eventually Has to Fix the Data

Authors- NameLars FredholmTwitter

Teams are teaching agents to navigate data platforms with skills, semantic layers, and ontologies. The results are impressive. They also keep running into the same thing: the data underneath.

``TL;DR:` Analytics agents are being improved by layering context around the data: skills, semantic layers, and lately ontologies. It works, but every such layer is still a map over a platform it did not shape. If the platform is ambiguous and messy, the map grows expensive, drifts out of date, and the agent may still ignore it. The more durable fix is a declarative data model that generates more of the platform, so meaning is built in rather than documented on top.

- The context arms race

- Where context hits a wall

- What the mess actually looks like

- Building the meaning into the model

- From context to structure

## The context arms race

The most visible recent development in agentic analytics is the context placed around the data: skills, semantic layers, rules files, reference docs, glossaries. Anthropic now automates 95% of its internal business analytics queries through Claude at roughly 95% accuracy, and credits skills as the biggest lever; without them, accuracy did not exceed 21%. Claire Gouze took her analytics agent from 4% to 82% correct answers by iterating on a dbt semantic layer and agent rules.

The context is also getting more formal. Open Semantic Interchange (OSI), the vendor-neutral semantic standard backed by Snowflake, dbt Labs, Salesforce, and other companies, now defines a common way to exchange semantic metadata across tools. It has also added an ontology specification: concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules. Microsoft is going the same way with Fabric IQ, now in preview, which makes ontology a core platform item for grounding agents. The docs are clear about why: tables and schemas are "structures built for machines, not meaning."

Skills, semantic layers, and ontologies differ in how formal they are, but they all respond to the same problem: the agent needs a map of the data estate. It needs to know what concepts exist, which tables matter, which joins are safe, which definitions are governed, and which traps to avoid.

A map is the obvious first move. You can draw one without changing the terrain.

## Where context hits a wall

The improvement from context is real. That is not the point in question.

The question is what the examples reveal after the first jump in accuracy. In both Anthropic's post and Gouze's semantic-layer experiment, the remaining work is not only about giving the agent more instructions. It is about improving the data model the agent is trying to use.

For Anthropic, the hard part is mapping a user's question to the right entities in the data model; once that works, writing the SQL is easy. Their stack uses skills to help the agent retrieve and follow the right context, but the foundation is still the governed data underneath: canonical datasets, deprecated near-duplicates, enforced standards, maintained metadata, freshness checks, and validation.

A semantic layer can help resolve which definition of revenue to use, but only after someone has done the work of defining, governing, and maintaining that choice. If forty plausible revenue datasets exist underneath, the semantic layer can route around the confusion, but it has not made the confusion disappear. What should be the same business decision now has to be represented in the warehouse, the semantic layer, the documentation, and the agent instructions, and all of those representations can drift.

Gouze ends up in the same place. Her remaining failures came from bad joins between tables that shared primary keys, nulls nobody filtered, business rules that existed only in people's heads, and metrics that needed data model changes before any semantic layer could express them. Her own summary: "the semantic layer reduces hallucinations, but doesn't remove them entirely."

Context can route an agent to the right answer only if the platform contains a right answer to route to.

## What the mess actually looks like

Anyone who has worked in a data platform that grew over many years knows what this looks like. Naming conventions vary from team to team and year to year. Keys are missing or loosely defined. Pipelines are orphaned. Some data is historized, some is overwritten in place, and nothing tells you which. Filters are undocumented, grain is mixed, and the same logic is implemented three times with three subtly different results.

Each of these quirks turns into context the agent has to carry around. Anthropic's published skill skeleton includes a dedicated "Field Naming Gotchas" section ("use `field_x_v2` NOT `field_x`"). This is compensating documentation: writing the mess down instead of removing it.

Documentation like that has several problems. The first is that it goes stale. Anthropic watched accuracy fall from roughly 95% to 65% within a month, because the docs described a model that changed daily, and it took real engineering (colocated docs, CI hooks, automated correction harvesting) to stop the rot.

It is also expensive, since every gotcha means more tokens for the agent to read on every question; Gouze found her semantic-layer setup noticeably slower and costlier. It crowds out other context, which feeds the very retrieval failures it was meant to prevent. And in the end it is advice rather than a rule. In Anthropic's most telling experiment, the agent had access to thousands of earlier SQL queries, demonstrably read them, and accuracy moved by less than a point.

`A rule the agent has to remember is weaker than a rule the platform enforces.

A formal ontology does better than free-text documentation. It is harder to misread, and its constraints can be checked. But declared over a messy platform, it still has to encode the mess, and it still describes a territory it did not shape.

Context is useful. But when it is compensating for ambiguity, duplicated logic, missing keys, unclear grain, or undocumented business rules, the better long-term answer is not more context. It is a better governed model, one that embeds and enforces more of that meaning natively.

## Building the meaning into the model

The way to get there is to declare meaning from the beginning and let more of the platform be generated from it.

Define the business model declaratively: entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules that turn source data into analytical facts. Then let a compiler generate the physical implementation.

This changes the failure mode. Much of the mess described earlier never gets a chance to form. Naming is uniform because it is generated. Every entity gets identifiers from the start. Historization is something you declare, with one mechanism everywhere, rather than something each pipeline solves in its own way. Grain is fixed per entity, and attributes are modeled as answers to atomic business questions: a loan amount is not just a number, but a number plus a currency. Logic is defined once and compiled wherever it is needed, and nothing deployed can be orphaned, because everything derives from the current model.

None of this solves everything. A generated platform still inherits the quality of its source systems, and a poorly chosen model compiles just as reliably as a good one. But it shrinks the space where mess can accumulate, and the description and the implementation can no longer drift apart, because one is produced from the other.

For an agent, that last point is the one that counts. Coding agents do well because codebases are legible, and a generated platform is legible by construction: an agent that learns the shape of one entity knows the shape of all of them. The declared model is the source and the warehouse is an output. In effect, the model becomes the ontology, except the platform is generated from it instead of merely described by it. A semantic layer can be exposed from the same declarations rather than maintained on the side.

## From context to structure

This is the idea behind Daana, a declarative data modeling tool: business models defined in YAML, compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure, with identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, and documentation generated rather than hand-maintained. We recently documented what this looks like in practice in a case study with Nextory: a platform rebuilt so that definitions drive the implementation, and what changed once meaning lived in the model instead of in documentation beside it.

With that kind of approach, much of the ambiguity we see in today's platforms never gets the chance to form. The platform becomes easier for humans to understand, easier for agents to navigate, and easier to extend without slowly recreating the same mess in a new layer.

`Context that explains a well-structured platform is leverage. Context that papers over an ambiguous one is a patch.

The patch grows with every gotcha and decays with every schema change. The lasting gains come from moving meaning out of the map and into the territory.

Or, put more bluntly: rather than writing ever better guidebooks to the maze, stop building mazes.

Discuss on Twitter • View on GitHub

`Load Comments

input.title: Context Isn't Enough: Agentic Analytics Eventually Has to Fix the Data
input.thesis: Teams are improving analytics agents by layering context around the data — skills, semantic layers, rules files, and now formal ontologies (OSI, Microsoft Fabric IQ) — and it demonstrably works (Anthropic: 21% → ~95%; Claire Gouze: 4% → 82%). But every such layer is a map over a platform it did not shape: it goes stale, costs tokens on every question, crowds out other context, and remains advice rather than an enforced rule, so residual failures come from the data model itself (bad joins on shared primary keys, unfiltered nulls, business rules living in people's heads, metrics requiring model changes). The post argues the durable fix is to declare the business model — entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules turning source data into analytical facts — and let a compiler generate the physical platform, so naming, identifiers, historization, grain, validation and documentation are built in rather than documented on top. The declared model becomes the ontology and the warehouse becomes its output; a semantic layer can be exposed from the same declarations instead of maintained beside them. This is presented as the idea behind Daana (YAML business models compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure).

mandates.claim: "Define the business model declaratively: entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules that turn source data into analytical facts. Then let a compiler generate the physical implementation."
mandates.implication: The DAB focal model is the ONLY hand-authored surface, and it must be able to express all seven of those element kinds. Physical DDL, transformations and pipeline code are compiler output — a builder writes model declarations, not SQL files.

mandates.claim: "The declared model is the source and the warehouse is an output."
mandates.implication: The warehouse is regenerable and disposable. No hand-edits to deployed objects; any change starts in the declaration and is re-compiled. Round-tripping fixes back from the warehouse into the model is excluded.

mandates.claim: "Naming is uniform because it is generated."
mandates.implication: Table/column naming must be produced by the generator from the model, not by team convention or hand-written style guides. Naming rules live in the compiler; no per-source or per-team naming dialects survive into DAS/DAB/DAR.

mandates.claim: "Every entity gets identifiers from the start."
mandates.implication: Identifier declaration is mandatory, not retrofitted. An entity with no declared identity should not be a legal model — this forecloses the "keys are missing or loosely defined" failure the post lists.

mandates.claim: "Historization is something you declare, with one mechanism everywhere, rather than something each pipeline solves in its own way."
mandates.implication: One single historization mechanism across the whole platform, selected by declaration per entity/source. Rules out a mix of historized tables and overwrite-in-place tables where "nothing tells you which" — so per-pipeline load-strategy choices (including at the ingestion tool level) must be driven by the model, not configured independently.

mandates.claim: "Grain is fixed per entity"
mandates.implication: Grain is a declared property of an entity, enforced by the compiler. Mixed-grain tables must be structurally impossible rather than documented as a gotcha.

mandates.claim: "attributes are modeled as answers to atomic business questions: a loan amount is not just a number, but a number plus a currency"
mandates.implication: Attributes carry their full semantic payload (value + unit/currency) as one modeled thing. A bare numeric column is an under-specified attribute; the attribute type system must support composite, unit-bearing values.

mandates.claim: "Logic is defined once and compiled wherever it is needed"
mandates.implication: A rule is authored in exactly one place and fanned out by the compiler into every layer that needs it. Re-implementing the same logic in DAS, DAB and DAR (the post's "same logic implemented three times with three subtly different results") is the failure mode being designed out.

mandates.claim: "nothing deployed can be orphaned, because everything derives from the current model"
mandates.implication: Deployment is a complete projection of the current model: objects not derived from it are removed or reconciled. No orphaned pipelines or leftover tables from previous model versions.

mandates.claim: "A semantic layer can be exposed from the same declarations rather than maintained on the side."
mandates.implication: The requirements/serving layer (and any semantic layer or star schema) is generated from the DAB declarations. Maintaining a parallel semantic-layer definition is precisely the drift the post warns about.

mandates.claim: "In effect, the model becomes the ontology, except the platform is generated from it instead of merely described by it."
mandates.implication: Do not build a separate ontology artifact over the platform. If ontology-shaped output is needed (concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules), emit it from the model.

mandates.claim: "with identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, and documentation generated rather than hand-maintained" (Daana: "business models defined in YAML, compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure")
mandates.implication: Five specific outputs must be generator responsibilities, not human ones: identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, documentation. The authoring format named is YAML; the compile target is deployed transformation infrastructure.

mandates.claim: "A rule the agent has to remember is weaker than a rule the platform enforces."
mandates.implication: Whenever a constraint is expressible in the model, express it there instead of in agent instructions/skills/rules files. Agent-facing prose is the last resort, not the first.

mandates.claim: "Context can route an agent to the right answer only if the platform contains a right answer to route to." / "If forty plausible revenue datasets exist underneath, the semantic layer can route around the confusion, but it has not made the confusion disappear."
mandates.implication: Resolve duplicate and near-duplicate definitions in the model rather than routing around them downstream. A single business decision must have one representation, not one each in the warehouse, semantic layer, docs and agent instructions.

mandates.claim: Compensating documentation "goes stale" (Anthropic's accuracy fell "from roughly 95% to 65% within a month"), "is also expensive, since every gotcha means more tokens for the agent to read on every question", "crowds out other context", "and in the end it is advice rather than a rule."
mandates.implication: Do not budget a growing "gotchas" document as the fix for platform ambiguity; each of the four costs (staleness, tokens, crowd-out, non-enforcement) applies. If any hand-maintained context remains, the post names what it took to stop the rot: colocated docs, CI hooks, automated correction harvesting.

mandates.claim: "None of this solves everything. A generated platform still inherits the quality of its source systems, and a poorly chosen model compiles just as reliably as a good one."
mandates.implication: Generation guarantees consistency, not correctness. Source-data quality (the DAS input) and modeling judgment (the DAB design) still need human review and governance — the compiler will not catch a bad model.

mandates.claim: "the description and the implementation can no longer drift apart, because one is produced from the other"
mandates.implication: Non-drift is the design goal to preserve: any feature that lets documentation, semantic definitions or agent context be edited independently of the model reintroduces the problem the architecture exists to remove.

mandates.claim: "a generated platform is legible by construction: an agent that learns the shape of one entity knows the shape of all of them"
mandates.implication: Uniformity across entities is an agent-facing feature, not cosmetics. Per-entity special cases, escape hatches and bespoke overrides erode the property that makes the platform navigable.

mandates.claim: Anthropic's stack "uses skills to help the agent retrieve and follow the right context, but the foundation is still the governed data underneath: canonical datasets, deprecated near-duplicates, enforced standards, maintained metadata, freshness checks, and validation."
mandates.implication: Even a generated platform needs the governance list named here — canonical designation, explicit deprecation of near-duplicates, enforced standards, metadata, freshness checks, validation. Generation does not remove the need for these; it changes where they are declared.

mandates.claim: "For Anthropic, the hard part is mapping a user's question to the right entities in the data model; once that works, writing the SQL is easy."
mandates.implication: Optimize the serving layer for question-to-entity mapping (unambiguous, well-identified entities), not for SQL generation ergonomics. SQL generation is not the bottleneck being solved.

openQuestions: Which single historization mechanism? The post mandates "one mechanism everywhere" but never names it (no SCD type, no validity-interval scheme, no bitemporal-vs-unitemporal choice).

What form does the generated semantic layer take? The post says it "can be exposed from the same declarations" but does not say in what format or against which interface — OSI, dbt, Fabric IQ, or a star schema are all left open.

Whether to emit or interoperate with the OSI ontology specification (concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules). The post says "the model becomes the ontology" but does not say whether the model should serialize to OSI or ignore it.
How is model quality reviewed? "A poorly chosen model compiles just as reliably as a good one" identifies the gap but proposes no review process, linting, or modeling methodology to close it.

How the governance list (canonical datasets, deprecated near-duplicates, enforced standards, maintained metadata, freshness checks, validation) is expressed in a declarative model — the post says the foundation is still governed data, but not which of those become YAML declarations versus separate process.

What generation cannot fix at the source boundary: "a generated platform still inherits the quality of its source systems" — the post gives no guidance on where source-quality handling (nulls, loose keys, missing history) lives relative to the declared model.

What context is still worth writing over a generated platform. "Context that explains a well-structured platform is leverage" — but the post never says what that residual context contains, how much, or where it lives.
The general attribute type system beyond the loan-amount-plus-currency illustration: which atomic business questions get first-class composite types is not specified.

How the mandates map onto a three-layer DAS/DAB/DAR split — the post argues at the level of "the model" and "the platform" and never names layers, so the placement of identifiers, historization and grain across the three layers is a builder decision.
How to migrate an existing messy platform. The post's advice is "stop building mazes" but it offers no path from the existing estate to the generated one beyond the Nextory case study reference.

data.title: Context Isn't Enough: Agentic Analytics Eventually Has to Fix the Data
data.thesis: Teams are improving analytics agents by layering context around the data — skills, semantic layers, rules files, and now formal ontologies (OSI, Microsoft Fabric IQ) — and it demonstrably works (Anthropic: 21% → ~95%; Claire Gouze: 4% → 82%). But every such layer is a map over a platform it did not shape: it goes stale, costs tokens on every question, crowds out other context, and remains advice rather than an enforced rule, so residual failures come from the data model itself (bad joins on shared primary keys, unfiltered nulls, business rules living in people's heads, metrics requiring model changes). The post argues the durable fix is to declare the business model — entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules turning source data into analytical facts — and let a compiler generate the physical platform, so naming, identifiers, historization, grain, validation and documentation are built in rather than documented on top. The declared model becomes the ontology and the warehouse becomes its output; a semantic layer can be exposed from the same declarations instead of maintained beside them. This is presented as the idea behind Daana (YAML business models compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure).

mandates.claim: "Define the business model declaratively: entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules that turn source data into analytical facts. Then let a compiler generate the physical implementation."
mandates.implication: The DAB focal model is the ONLY hand-authored surface, and it must be able to express all seven of those element kinds. Physical DDL, transformations and pipeline code are compiler output — a builder writes model declarations, not SQL files.

mandates.claim: "The declared model is the source and the warehouse is an output."
mandates.implication: The warehouse is regenerable and disposable. No hand-edits to deployed objects; any change starts in the declaration and is re-compiled. Round-tripping fixes back from the warehouse into the model is excluded.

mandates.claim: "Naming is uniform because it is generated."
mandates.implication: Table/column naming must be produced by the generator from the model, not by team convention or hand-written style guides. Naming rules live in the compiler; no per-source or per-team naming dialects survive into DAS/DAB/DAR.

mandates.claim: "Every entity gets identifiers from the start."
mandates.implication: Identifier declaration is mandatory, not retrofitted. An entity with no declared identity should not be a legal model — this forecloses the "keys are missing or loosely defined" failure the post lists.

mandates.claim: "Historization is something you declare, with one mechanism everywhere, rather than something each pipeline solves in its own way."
mandates.implication: One single historization mechanism across the whole platform, selected by declaration per entity/source. Rules out a mix of historized tables and overwrite-in-place tables where "nothing tells you which" — so per-pipeline load-strategy choices (including at the ingestion tool level) must be driven by the model, not configured independently.

mandates.claim: "Grain is fixed per entity"
mandates.implication: Grain is a declared property of an entity, enforced by the compiler. Mixed-grain tables must be structurally impossible rather than documented as a gotcha.

mandates.claim: "attributes are modeled as answers to atomic business questions: a loan amount is not just a number, but a number plus a currency"
mandates.implication: Attributes carry their full semantic payload (value + unit/currency) as one modeled thing. A bare numeric column is an under-specified attribute; the attribute type system must support composite, unit-bearing values.

mandates.claim: "Logic is defined once and compiled wherever it is needed"
mandates.implication: A rule is authored in exactly one place and fanned out by the compiler into every layer that needs it. Re-implementing the same logic in DAS, DAB and DAR (the post's "same logic implemented three times with three subtly different results") is the failure mode being designed out.

mandates.claim: "nothing deployed can be orphaned, because everything derives from the current model"
mandates.implication: Deployment is a complete projection of the current model: objects not derived from it are removed or reconciled. No orphaned pipelines or leftover tables from previous model versions.

mandates.claim: "A semantic layer can be exposed from the same declarations rather than maintained on the side."
mandates.implication: The requirements/serving layer (and any semantic layer or star schema) is generated from the DAB declarations. Maintaining a parallel semantic-layer definition is precisely the drift the post warns about.

mandates.claim: "In effect, the model becomes the ontology, except the platform is generated from it instead of merely described by it."
mandates.implication: Do not build a separate ontology artifact over the platform. If ontology-shaped output is needed (concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules), emit it from the model.

mandates.claim: "with identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, and documentation generated rather than hand-maintained" (Daana: "business models defined in YAML, compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure")
mandates.implication: Five specific outputs must be generator responsibilities, not human ones: identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, documentation. The authoring format named is YAML; the compile target is deployed transformation infrastructure.

mandates.claim: "A rule the agent has to remember is weaker than a rule the platform enforces."
mandates.implication: Whenever a constraint is expressible in the model, express it there instead of in agent instructions/skills/rules files. Agent-facing prose is the last resort, not the first.

mandates.claim: "Context can route an agent to the right answer only if the platform contains a right answer to route to." / "If forty plausible revenue datasets exist underneath, the semantic layer can route around the confusion, but it has not made the confusion disappear."
mandates.implication: Resolve duplicate and near-duplicate definitions in the model rather than routing around them downstream. A single business decision must have one representation, not one each in the warehouse, semantic layer, docs and agent instructions.

mandates.claim: Compensating documentation "goes stale" (Anthropic's accuracy fell "from roughly 95% to 65% within a month"), "is also expensive, since every gotcha means more tokens for the agent to read on every question", "crowds out other context", "and in the end it is advice rather than a rule."
mandates.implication: Do not budget a growing "gotchas" document as the fix for platform ambiguity; each of the four costs (staleness, tokens, crowd-out, non-enforcement) applies. If any hand-maintained context remains, the post names what it took to stop the rot: colocated docs, CI hooks, automated correction harvesting.

mandates.claim: "None of this solves everything. A generated platform still inherits the quality of its source systems, and a poorly chosen model compiles just as reliably as a good one."
mandates.implication: Generation guarantees consistency, not correctness. Source-data quality (the DAS input) and modeling judgment (the DAB design) still need human review and governance — the compiler will not catch a bad model.

mandates.claim: "the description and the implementation can no longer drift apart, because one is produced from the other"
mandates.implication: Non-drift is the design goal to preserve: any feature that lets documentation, semantic definitions or agent context be edited independently of the model reintroduces the problem the architecture exists to remove.

mandates.claim: "a generated platform is legible by construction: an agent that learns the shape of one entity knows the shape of all of them"
mandates.implication: Uniformity across entities is an agent-facing feature, not cosmetics. Per-entity special cases, escape hatches and bespoke overrides erode the property that makes the platform navigable.

mandates.claim: Anthropic's stack "uses skills to help the agent retrieve and follow the right context, but the foundation is still the governed data underneath: canonical datasets, deprecated near-duplicates, enforced standards, maintained metadata, freshness checks, and validation."
mandates.implication: Even a generated platform needs the governance list named here — canonical designation, explicit deprecation of near-duplicates, enforced standards, metadata, freshness checks, validation. Generation does not remove the need for these; it changes where they are declared.

mandates.claim: "For Anthropic, the hard part is mapping a user's question to the right entities in the data model; once that works, writing the SQL is easy."
mandates.implication: Optimize the serving layer for question-to-entity mapping (unambiguous, well-identified entities), not for SQL generation ergonomics. SQL generation is not the bottleneck being solved.

artifacts.name: YAML
artifacts.detail: Daana is "a declarative data modeling tool: business models defined in YAML, compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure". YAML is the only file format named in the post. No YAML keys, key names, or schema fragments appear anywhere in the post.

artifacts.name: entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules that turn source data into analytical facts
artifacts.detail: The seven kinds of thing the declarative business model must contain: "Define the business model declaratively: entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules that turn source data into analytical facts." This is the closest the post comes to a model schema.

artifacts.name: identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, and documentation
artifacts.detail: The five things Daana generates rather than hand-maintains: "...with identifiers, historization, naming consistency, validation, and documentation generated rather than hand-maintained."

artifacts.name: Daana
artifacts.detail: "a declarative data modeling tool: business models defined in YAML, compiled into deployed transformation infrastructure". No CLI name, commands or flags are given in the post.

artifacts.name: field_x_v2` NOT `field_x`
artifacts.detail: Cited from Anthropic's published skill skeleton, which "includes a dedicated \"Field Naming Gotchas\" section (\"use `field_x_v2` NOT `field_x`\")". The post calls this "compensating documentation: writing the mess down instead of removing it" — i.e. the exact naming situation a generated platform must make impossible.

artifacts.name: Field Naming Gotchas
artifacts.detail: A "dedicated" section in Anthropic's published skill skeleton. Named as the canonical example of documenting mess instead of removing it.

artifacts.name: a loan amount is not just a number, but a number plus a currency
artifacts.detail: The post's only concrete typing example: "attributes are modeled as answers to atomic business questions: a loan amount is not just a number, but a number plus a currency." No general type-mapping table is given.

artifacts.name: Open Semantic Interchange (OSI)
artifacts.detail: "the vendor-neutral semantic standard backed by Snowflake, dbt Labs, Salesforce, and other companies, now defines a common way to exchange semantic metadata across tools. It has also added an ontology specification: concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules."

artifacts.name: concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules
artifacts.detail: The five things OSI's ontology specification covers. Relevant because the post claims "the model becomes the ontology" — a declarative model is expected to cover comparable ground.

artifacts.name: Fabric IQ
artifacts.detail: Microsoft, "now in preview, which makes ontology a core platform item for grounding agents."

artifacts.name: dbt semantic layer
artifacts.detail: Claire Gouze "took her analytics agent from 4% to 82% correct answers by iterating on a dbt semantic layer and agent rules." Her summary quoted: "the semantic layer reduces hallucinations, but doesn't remove them entirely."

artifacts.name: canonical datasets, deprecated near-duplicates, enforced standards, maintained metadata, freshness checks, and validation
artifacts.detail: Named as "the foundation ... the governed data underneath" in Anthropic's stack, which skills sit on top of.

artifacts.name: colocated docs, CI hooks, automated correction harvesting
artifacts.detail: "it took real engineering (colocated docs, CI hooks, automated correction harvesting) to stop the rot" after Anthropic's accuracy fell from ~95% to 65% within a month.

artifacts.name: 95% / ~95% / 21% / 65% / 4% → 82% / "less than a point"
artifacts.detail: Anthropic automates 95% of internal business analytics queries at roughly 95% accuracy; without skills accuracy "did not exceed 21%"; accuracy fell to roughly 65% within a month as docs went stale; Gouze went 4% → 82%; an agent with access to thousands of earlier SQL queries that "demonstrably read them" moved accuracy "by less than a point."

artifacts.name: Nextory case study
artifacts.detail: "We recently documented what this looks like in practice in a case study with Nextory: a platform rebuilt so that definitions drive the implementation, and what changed once meaning lived in the model instead of in documentation beside it."

artifacts.name: the mess inventory
artifacts.detail: What a generated platform must prevent: "Naming conventions vary from team to team and year to year. Keys are missing or loosely defined. Pipelines are orphaned. Some data is historized, some is overwritten in place, and nothing tells you which. Filters are undocumented, grain is mixed, and the same logic is implemented three times with three subtly different results." Plus Gouze's residual failures: "bad joins between tables that shared primary keys, nulls nobody filtered, business rules that existed only in people's heads, and metrics that needed data model changes before any semantic layer could express them."

artifacts.name: NOT PRESENT
artifacts.detail: The post never mentions DAS, DAB, DAR, dlt, daana-cli, Unified Star Schema, any CLI command or flag, any schema/table/column name, any SQL construct, any directory layout, or any source-to-target type mapping. Everything above is the full inventory of named things.

quotes: Define the business model declaratively: entities, attributes, identifiers, relationships, valid histories, source mappings, and the rules that turn source data into analytical facts.

Naming is uniform because it is generated. Every entity gets identifiers from the start. Historization is something you declare, with one mechanism everywhere, rather than something each pipeline solves in its own way.
Grain is fixed per entity, and attributes are modeled as answers to atomic business questions: a loan amount is not just a number, but a number plus a currency.
Logic is defined once and compiled wherever it is needed, and nothing deployed can be orphaned, because everything derives from the current model.

The declared model is the source and the warehouse is an output. In effect, the model becomes the ontology, except the platform is generated from it instead of merely described by it. A semantic layer can be exposed from the same declarations rather than maintained on the side.
A rule the agent has to remember is weaker than a rule the platform enforces.
Context can route an agent to the right answer only if the platform contains a right answer to route to.
A generated platform still inherits the quality of its source systems, and a poorly chosen model compiles just as reliably as a good one.
openQuestions: Which single historization mechanism? The post mandates "one mechanism everywhere" but never names it (no SCD type, no validity-interval scheme, no bitemporal-vs-unitemporal choice).

What form does the generated semantic layer take? The post says it "can be exposed from the same declarations" but does not say in what format or against which interface — OSI, dbt, Fabric IQ, or a star schema are all left open.

Whether to emit or interoperate with the OSI ontology specification (concepts, typed relationships, identity declarations, constraints, derivation rules). The post says "the model becomes the ontology" but does not say whether the model should serialize to OSI or ignore it.
How is model quality reviewed? "A poorly chosen model compiles just as reliably as a good one" identifies the gap but proposes no review process, linting, or modeling methodology to close it.

How the governance list (canonical datasets, deprecated near-duplicates, enforced standards, maintained metadata, freshness checks, validation) is expressed in a declarative model — the post says the foundation is still governed data, but not which of those become YAML declarations versus separate process.

What generation cannot fix at the source boundary: "a generated platform still inherits the quality of its source systems" — the post gives no guidance on where source-quality handling (nulls, loose keys, missing history) lives relative to the declared model.

What context is still worth writing over a generated platform. "Context that explains a well-structured platform is leverage" — but the post never says what that residual context contains, how much, or where it lives.
The general attribute type system beyond the loan-amount-plus-currency illustration: which atomic business questions get first-class composite types is not specified.

How the mandates map onto a three-layer DAS/DAB/DAR split — the post argues at the level of "the model" and "the platform" and never names layers, so the placement of identifiers, historization and grain across the three layers is a builder decision.
How to migrate an existing messy platform. The post's advice is "stop building mazes" but it offers no path from the existing estate to the generated one beyond the Nextory case study reference.
